name: Curcumin
text:
Curcumin is the bright yellow pigment of turmeric, obtained from the rhizomes of the plant Curcuma longa. Chemically it is a polyphenol of the curcuminoid group.

As a food additive it gives an orange-yellow colour and is used, for example, in curry powders, mustard, butter and cheese. It dissolves poorly in water.

name: Riboflavins
text:
Riboflavin is vitamin B2. In pure form it is a yellow-orange crystalline powder, and besides being a vitamin it is used as a food colour. It occurs naturally in meat, fish, eggs, dairy products and green vegetables.

Commercial riboflavin is now made mainly by fermentation with fungi and genetically modified bacteria. The additive has two forms: riboflavin itself, E101(i), and riboflavin-5'-phosphate, E101(ii), which dissolves better in water. Riboflavin is also added to flour and breakfast cereals to enrich them.

name: Tartrazine
text:
Tartrazine is a synthetic lemon-yellow azo dye, known in the US as FD&C Yellow 5. It is used in soft drinks, sweets, desserts, snacks, sauces and many other processed foods, and combined with Brilliant Blue FCF or Green S it gives shades of green.

In the EU, foods containing it must carry the warning that it may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children. According to the US FDA, it causes hives in fewer than 1 in 10,000 people.

name: Alkannin
text:
Alkannin is a natural red-brown pigment obtained from the roots of dyer's alkanet (Alkanna tinctoria), a plant of the Mediterranean region. Chemically it is a naphthoquinone derivative.

It is used as a food colouring and in cosmetics. It is deep red in acidic conditions and blue in alkaline ones.

name: Quinoline Yellow
text:
Quinoline Yellow WS is a synthetic water-soluble dye that gives a greenish-yellow colour. It is used in drinks and in foods such as sauces, decorations and coatings.

In the EU, foods containing it must carry the warning that it may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children. In 2009 EFSA lowered its acceptable daily intake from 10 to 0.5 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Fast Yellow AB
text: Fast Yellow AB is a synthetic yellow azo dye that was formerly used as a food colour under the number E105. It is no longer used in food. It has been implicated in non-atopic asthma.

name: Riboflavin-5'-phosphate sodium
text:
Riboflavin-5'-phosphate sodium is the sodium salt of riboflavin-5'-phosphate, a phosphate ester of vitamin B2 (riboflavin). It is used as a food colour, dissolves in water better than riboflavin itself and is quickly converted to free riboflavin after it is eaten.

It is also used to fortify flour with vitamin B2.

In EU law and in the international Codex numbering system this substance is not numbered E106: it is listed as form (ii) of E101 (riboflavins).

name: Yellow 2G
text: Yellow 2G is a synthetic yellow azo dye that has been used as a food colouring under the number E107 (colour index CI 18965). It is a yellow powder that dissolves in water.

name: Sunset Yellow FCF
text:
Sunset Yellow FCF, also called Orange Yellow S and, in the US, FD&C Yellow 6, is a synthetic orange azo dye derived from petroleum. It is used in sweets, desserts, snacks, sauces and preserved fruits, and together with amaranth (E123) to give a brown colour to chocolate and caramel products.

In the EU, foods containing it must carry the warning that it may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.

name: Orange GGN
text: Orange GGN, also known as alpha-naphthol orange, is a synthetic orange azo dye that was formerly used as a food colour. In Europe it has been prohibited in food since 1 January 1978, and it has never been included in the Codex Alimentarius list of food additives.

name: Carmine
text:
Carmine is a bright red pigment made from carminic acid, which is extracted from cochineal and some other scale insects: the powdered insect bodies are boiled and the extract is precipitated with alum. It is also known as cochineal, cochineal extract or Natural Red 4. Because it comes from insects, it is not suitable for vegetarians or vegans.

It is used in yoghurt, sweets, gelatin desserts, meat products and drinks, including fruit juices. Carmine can cause allergic reactions in some people.

name: Citrus Red 2
text:
Citrus Red 2 is a synthetic azo dye that does not dissolve in water but dissolves readily in many organic solvents. Its food use is very narrow: in the United States it has been used since 1956 to colour the skin of some oranges, at no more than 2 mg per kg of fruit.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies it as possibly carcinogenic to humans (group 2B).

name: Azorubine (carmoisine)
text:
Azorubine, also called carmoisine, is a synthetic red azo dye. It is mainly used in foods that are heat-treated after fermentation; examples include some cheeses, dried fruit and some alcoholic drinks.

In the EU, foods containing it must carry the warning that it may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children. EFSA re-evaluated it in 2009 and kept its acceptable daily intake at 4 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Amaranth
text:
Amaranth, also known as FD&C Red No. 2, is a synthetic red azo dye. It has nothing to do with the amaranth plant apart from the name, which was taken from the red-coloured amaranth grain. It is used in foods and cosmetics; in the United Kingdom it is best known for colouring glacé cherries.

In the United States, the FDA ended its listing as a colour for food, drugs and cosmetics in 1976, stating that it did so to protect public health.

name: Ponceau 4R
text:
Ponceau 4R, also called Cochineal Red A or Brilliant Scarlet 4R, is a synthetic strawberry-red azo dye. Despite one of its names, it is not made from cochineal insects. It is stable to light, heat and acid but fades in the presence of ascorbic acid (vitamin C).

In the EU, foods containing it must carry the warning that it may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.

name: Ponceau SX
text: Ponceau SX, also called Scarlet GN or FD&C Red No. 4, is a synthetic red azo dye that was once used as a food colour. In the EU it was allowed in food until the end of 1976. Today it is mainly used in cosmetics such as shampoos, bubble baths and liquid soaps.

name: Ponceau 6R
text: Ponceau 6R, also called crystal ponceau 6R or crystal scarlet, is a synthetic red azo dye that was formerly used as a food colour under the number E126. It is also used in histology to stain fibrin, and it is closely related to the dye amaranth (E123).

name: Erythrosine
text:
Erythrosine, also known as FD&C Red No. 3, is a synthetic red-pink dye containing iodine; chemically it is the disodium salt of tetraiodofluorescein. It is used in sweets, ice pops, cake-decorating gels and especially cherries, and also in printing inks and dental plaque disclosing agents.

Studies linked high doses to thyroid tumours in male rats. The US FDA considers that the dye is probably not genotoxic and that these tumours have limited relevance to humans, but US law does not allow colour additives that cause cancer in animals. In January 2025 the FDA therefore revoked its use in food, effective 15 January 2027.

name: Red 2G
text: Red 2G is a synthetic red azo dye. In the EU it was used only in breakfast sausages and burger meat containing cereal or vegetables. In July 2007 EFSA concluded that it may be carcinogenic because it is converted to aniline in the body, and the European Commission suspended its use as a food colour the same month. It is also used in inks and paper.

name: Allura Red AC
text:
Allura Red AC, also known as FD&C Red 40, is a synthetic red azo dye. It was developed in 1971 as a replacement for amaranth and is now the most widely used red food dye in the United States. It is found in soft drinks, sweets, cotton candy, cherry-flavoured products, dairy products and some medicines.

In the EU, foods containing it must carry the warning that it may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.

name: Indanthrene blue RS
text: Indanthrene blue RS (indanthrone) is a synthetic dark blue anthraquinone dye first made by BASF in 1901. It is mainly a vat dye for cotton and other cellulose textiles and a pigment for paints and enamels, valued for its colour fastness. It has been assigned the food colour number E130.

name: Patent Blue V
text:
Patent Blue V is a synthetic sky-blue triphenylmethane dye. It is not widely used in food; in Europe it may be found in Scotch eggs, some jelly sweets, blue Curaçao and some gelatin desserts. In medicine it is used to stain lymph vessels.

Health authorities in some countries suspect that it may cause allergic reactions, from itching and rash to, rarely, anaphylactic shock.

name: Indigotine (indigo carmine)
text: Indigotine, also called indigo carmine or FD&C Blue No. 2, is made from indigo by sulfonation, which makes it water-soluble. Like indigo, it gives a blue colour, and it is one of the few blue food colours. It is also used in pharmaceutical capsules and cosmetics, as a pH indicator, and in medicine as a contrast agent and stain.

name: Brilliant Blue FCF
text:
Brilliant Blue FCF, also known as FD&C Blue No. 1, is a synthetic blue triarylmethane dye. Combined with tartrazine (E102) it gives shades of green. It is used in ice cream, sweets, icings, soft drinks, dairy products, canned processed peas, packet soups and the liqueur blue Curaçao, as well as in cosmetics.

In studies on rodents it was poorly absorbed from the gut, and most of it was excreted.

name: Chlorophylls and chlorophyllins
text:
Chlorophylls are the green pigments of plants. Chlorophyllins are water-soluble salts made from chlorophyll; the sodium chlorophyllins used as additives keep the original magnesium at their centre. The pigments are extracted from plant material such as grass, lucerne (alfalfa) and nettle.

Chlorophyll itself does not dissolve in water, so it is first mixed with a little vegetable oil. It is used to colour foods and drinks green, for example pasta and spirits.

name: Copper complexes of chlorophylls and chlorophyllins
text: Copper complexes of chlorophylls and chlorophyllins are green colours made from chlorophyll extracted from plants such as grass, lucerne (alfalfa) and nettle, in which copper takes the place of the magnesium of the natural pigment. The chlorophyll form dissolves in oil; the chlorophyllin form is made into water-soluble sodium and potassium salts and is supplied as a dark green powder or solution.

name: Green S
text: Green S, also known as Food Green S or lissamine green B, is a synthetic green triarylmethane dye. It is used in foods such as mint sauce, desserts, gravy granules, sweets, ice cream and tinned peas. Because it can stain living cells, it is also used in ophthalmology to diagnose disorders of the eye surface, such as dry eye.

name: Fast Green FCF
text: Fast Green FCF, also known as FD&C Green No. 3, is a synthetic turquoise triarylmethane dye used as a food colour. It is poorly absorbed from the gut. A 2017 re-evaluation published by the WHO found it to have low toxicity and to be neither carcinogenic nor genotoxic. It is also used as a stain in histology and for proteins in laboratory analysis.

name: Plain caramel
text:
Plain caramel (caramel colour class I, also called caustic or spirit caramel) is a brown colour made by controlled heating of carbohydrates with an acid or alkali, without the ammonium or sulphite compounds used for the other classes.

It is used in whisky and other spirits, biscuits, crackers and other baked goods, and juice concentrates.

name: Caustic sulphite caramel
text:
Caustic sulphite caramel (caramel colour class II) is a brown colour made by controlled heating of carbohydrates with sulphite compounds in the presence of an alkali. It has a mild flavour, a distinctly reddish tone and good stability in alcohol.

It is used in tea, wine, sherry, brandy, cognac, rum, whisky and some vinegars.

name: Ammonia caramel
text:
Ammonia caramel (caramel colour class III, also called baker's, confectioner's or beer caramel) is a red-brown colour made by controlled heating of carbohydrates with ammonium compounds.

It is used in beer, breakfast cereals, liquorice, confectionery, gravy and sauces such as soy and barbecue sauce.

name: Sulphite ammonia caramel
text:
Sulphite ammonia caramel (caramel colour class IV, also called soft-drink or acid-proof caramel) is a dark brown colour made by controlled heating of carbohydrates with both sulphite and ammonium compounds. It is stable in acidic conditions.

It is used in soft drinks such as colas, balsamic vinegar, coffee, chocolate syrups, sauces, soups and seasonings.

name: Brilliant Black PN
text: Brilliant Black PN, also called Brilliant Black BN or Black PN, is a synthetic black azo dye. It is used in food decorations and coatings, desserts, sweets, ice cream, mustard, red fruit jams, soft drinks, flavoured milk drinks, fish paste and lumpfish caviar.

name: Carbon black
text:
Carbon black is a black form of carbon produced by the incomplete combustion of petroleum products, coal tar or vegetable matter in a limited supply of air. It is used mainly as a colorant and reinforcing filler in tyres and other rubber products and as a pigment in plastics, paints and inks. In the international Codex numbering system, the number 152 denotes carbon black from hydrocarbon sources as a food colour.

In the EEC the number E152 originally belonged to a different substance, the synthetic azo dye Black 7984 (Food Black 2), which was deleted from the list of food colours from 1 January 1977.

name: Vegetable carbon
text:
Vegetable carbon is a black colour that consists essentially of finely divided carbon. It is made by carbonising plant material such as wood, coconut shells, bamboo or peat, followed by activation, washing, drying and grinding.

Among foods, it is used in liquorice and other sweets and in flavoured fermented milk products.

name: Brown FK
text:
Brown FK, also called kipper brown, is a mixture of six synthetic azo dyes with added sodium chloride and/or sodium sulfate. It is very soluble in water and gives a brown colour. It was once used in smoked and cured mackerel and other fish, including kippers, and in some cooked hams and other meats, because its colour did not fade during cooking.

In 2011 the European Food Safety Authority found that Brown FK was no longer used and that the toxicity data were too limited to conclude on its safety.

name: Brown HT
text: Brown HT, also called chocolate brown HT, is a synthetic brown diazo dye made from coal tar. It is used as a colour in place of cocoa or caramel, mainly in chocolate cakes, but also in desserts, biscuits, sweets, cheeses, yoghurts, jams, ice cream, breakfast cereals and other foods.

name: Carotenes
text:
Carotenes are orange and yellow pigments that give carrots their colour and occur in many other fruits and vegetables, in palm oil and in milk fat. Beta-carotene, the most common form, is converted in the body into vitamin A; alpha- and gamma-carotene have weaker vitamin A activity.

The additive is produced synthetically or from natural sources such as the fungus Blakeslea trispora or the alga Dunaliella salina. It colours products such as juices, cakes, desserts, butter and margarine.

name: Annatto
text:
Annatto is an orange natural colour extracted from the seeds of the achiote tree (Bixa orellana). Its main pigments are bixin, which is fat-soluble, and norbixin, which is water-soluble.

It is widely used to colour cheese, butter, margarine, snacks, smoked fish and breakfast cereals. Rare allergic reactions to annatto have been reported.

name: Paprika extract
text:
Paprika extract is a red natural colour obtained by solvent extraction from the fruits of the peppers Capsicum annuum or Capsicum frutescens; the solvents are removed before use. Its main colouring compounds are capsanthin and capsorubin, and it is much milder than capsicum oleoresin.

It is used in cheese, sausages, margarine, oils, sauces, snacks, drinks and desserts, and in poultry feed to deepen the colour of egg yolks.

name: Lycopene
text:
Lycopene is the bright red carotenoid pigment of tomatoes. It is also found in watermelon, pink grapefruit, pink guava, papaya and rose hips, and tomato products such as ketchup are the main dietary source. Unlike beta-carotene, it has no vitamin A activity.

Because of its strong colour, it is used as a food colouring.

name: Beta-apo-8'-carotenal
text:
Beta-apo-8'-carotenal (apocarotenal) is an orange to orange-red carotenoid found in spinach and citrus fruits. Like other carotenoids it is a precursor of vitamin A, with about half the provitamin A activity of beta-carotene.

It is used in fat-based foods such as margarine, sauces and salad dressings, and in drinks, dairy products and sweets.

name: Ethyl ester of beta-apo-8'-carotenic acid
text:
The ethyl ester of beta-apo-8'-carotenic acid, also called Food orange 7, is an orange-red carotenoid. It occurs in small quantities in some plants but has been produced commercially from beta-apo-8'-carotenal (E160e).

It was removed from the EU list of food additives in November 2011 because it was no longer being manufactured.

name: Flavoxanthin
text: Flavoxanthin is a natural golden-yellow xanthophyll, a type of carotenoid pigment, found in small quantities in a variety of plants. It is used as a food colour.

name: Lutein
text:
Lutein is a carotenoid pigment (a xanthophyll) made by plants and found in large amounts in green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale, as well as in egg yolks. It appears yellow at low concentrations and orange-red at high concentrations.

As a food additive it is extracted from the petals of the Mexican marigold (Tagetes erecta). It is used as a colour in foods and dietary supplements and is added to animal feed, for example to colour egg yolks.

name: Cryptoxanthin
text: Cryptoxanthin (beta-cryptoxanthin) is a natural carotenoid pigment of the xanthophyll class, closely related to beta-carotene. It has been found in orange rind, papaya, winter squashes such as butternut, Physalis fruits, apples, egg yolk and butter. The body converts it into vitamin A. It is also used to colour food.

name: Rubixanthin
text: Rubixanthin, also called natural yellow 27, is a natural xanthophyll (carotenoid) pigment with a red-orange colour, found in rose hips. It is used as a food colour.

name: Violaxanthin
text: Violaxanthin is an orange xanthophyll (carotenoid) pigment found in a variety of plants. Plants form it from zeaxanthin, and it takes part in the xanthophyll cycle, which helps them deal with excess light. It is used as a food colour.

name: Rhodoxanthin
text: Rhodoxanthin is a purple xanthophyll (carotenoid) pigment found in small quantities in a variety of plants, including the yew (Taxus baccata), and in the feathers of some birds. It is used as a food colour.

name: Canthaxanthin
text:
Canthaxanthin is a keto-carotenoid pigment widely distributed in nature. It was first isolated from edible mushrooms and has also been found in green algae, bacteria, crustaceans and fish. It is added to feed for farmed trout and salmon and for poultry.

In people who took very high amounts in sun-tanning pills, canthaxanthin crystals were deposited in the retina; the deposits disappeared after the pills were stopped.

The EU list of additives still contains E161g only because it is used to colour medicines; the list notes that it may not be used in any food category.

name: Zeaxanthin
text: Zeaxanthin is one of the most common carotenoids in nature. It is the main yellow pigment of maize and also gives colour to paprika, saffron and goji berries. It occurs in the leaves of most green plants, and together with lutein it is one of the two main carotenoids in the retina of the human eye. It is used as a food colour.

name: Citranaxanthin
text: Citranaxanthin is a carotenoid pigment. It has natural sources but is generally prepared synthetically. It is used as an animal feed additive to give a yellow colour to chicken fat and egg yolks.

name: Astaxanthin
text:
Astaxanthin is a red, fat-soluble carotenoid pigment. It is produced naturally by the microalga Haematococcus pluvialis, the yeast Xanthophyllomyces dendrorhous and some bacteria, and animals that feed on them, such as salmon, trout, shrimp, krill and flamingos, take on its red-orange colour.

Nearly all commercial astaxanthin for fish farming is made synthetically. It is used mainly as a feed additive to colour farmed salmon and egg yolks, and also as a dietary supplement.

name: Beetroot red
text:
Beetroot red is a red food colour obtained from beets, usually from beet juice extract; its main pigment is betanin. Its shade depends on pH, from bright bluish-red to blue-violet, and it breaks down in alkaline conditions.

Betanin is degraded by light, heat and oxygen, so it is used mainly in frozen products, products with a short shelf life and dry products. Its most common uses are ice cream and powdered soft drinks; it is also used in some sweets, soups, and tomato and bacon products.

name: Anthocyanins
text:
Anthocyanins are water-soluble plant pigments that give the red, purple, blue or black colours of blueberries, raspberries, blackcurrants, grapes, red cabbage, black carrots and many other plants. Their colour depends on acidity: red or pink in acidic conditions, purple near neutral and greenish-yellow in alkaline conditions.

They are used to colour foods and drinks. Red grape skin and blackcurrant extracts have a long history of use as food colours in Europe.

name: Gardenia yellow (saffron, crocin)
text:
The number 164 is used for yellow colours based on crocin and crocetin, the carotenoid pigments of saffron. In the international Codex numbering system it denotes gardenia yellow, a colour from the fruit of Gardenia jasminoides, which contains the same pigments; in Australia and New Zealand it denotes saffron, crocetin or crocin.

Saffron itself is a spice made from the dried crimson stigmas and styles of the saffron crocus (Crocus sativus); picrocrocin and safranal are responsible for its taste and aroma. The stigmas are harvested by hand, which makes saffron costly. The FAO/WHO expert committee JECFA regards saffron as a food rather than a food additive.

name: Calcium carbonate
text:
Calcium carbonate is a white compound found in rocks such as chalk, limestone and marble, and in eggshells and seashells. Food-grade calcium carbonate is made from pure quarried marble or is precipitated from calcium hydroxide with carbon dioxide.

As a food additive it is used as a colour, acidity regulator, anticaking agent and stabiliser, and as a firming agent in canned and bottled vegetables. It is a calcium source in some soy and almond drinks, and in the UK it is added by law to milled bread flour other than wholemeal.

name: Titanium dioxide
text:
Titanium dioxide is a white pigment produced mainly from the mineral ilmenite. It is the most widely used white pigment and gives whiteness and opacity to paints, plastics, paper, medicines, toothpaste and sunscreens. In food it has been used in sweets, chewing gum, chocolates, ice cream, pastries, frostings and some cheeses.

In 2021 the European Food Safety Authority concluded that it could no longer be considered safe as a food additive, because concerns about genotoxicity (damage to DNA) could not be ruled out. The EU then withdrew its authorisation for use in food in 2022.

name: Iron oxides and hydroxides
text: Iron oxides and hydroxides are inorganic pigments that are widespread in nature. They come in black, red and yellow forms and give earthy shades from yellow and orange through red and brown to black. They are inexpensive, strongly coloured and durable, and are used in paints, coatings and coloured concrete as well as to colour food.

name: Aluminium
text: Aluminium used as a food additive is the metal itself, which gives a silver to grey metallic colour. It is used as a decorative metallic coating on the outside of sugar confectionery.

name: Silver
text:
Silver used as a food colour is the pure metal, applied as a decorative coating. Examples are silver decorations on confectionery and chocolates, silver dragées used on cakes, biscuits and other desserts, and the thin silver foil called vark used on South Asian sweets. It is also used in liqueurs.

In 2025 the European Food Safety Authority reported that the available data were insufficient to conclude on the safety of silver as a food additive.

name: Gold
text:
Gold used as a food additive is high-purity metallic gold applied as leaf, flakes or powder, purely for decoration, for example on chocolates, sweets, cakes and desserts and in liqueurs such as Danziger Goldwasser. Metallic gold is chemically inert: it has no taste, provides no nutrition, is not absorbed during digestion and leaves the body unaltered.

In its 2016 re-evaluation, EFSA noted that the additive may contain minute amounts of gold nanoparticles, which have shown genotoxicity in mammalian cells in laboratory tests.

name: Litholrubine BK
text: Litholrubine BK (Lithol Rubine BK, also called Pigment Rubine) is a reddish synthetic azo dye, usually supplied as a calcium salt. As a food colour it is used to colour cheese rind. It is also used to dye plastics, paints and printing inks, where it is a standard magenta, and in some lip balms.

name: Tannin
text: Tannins are astringent plant polyphenols that bind to and precipitate proteins. They are abundant in oak bark and cause the dry, puckering feeling in the mouth after unripe fruit, red wine or tea. Tannic acid, a specific tannin, is a yellow to light brown powder usually extracted from tara pods, gallnuts or sumac leaves.

name: Orcein
text:
Orcein is a dye extracted from several species of lichen, mainly Roccella tinctoria. Orcinol from the lichens is converted into orcein by ammonia and air. Orcein is reddish-brown, while the related lichen dye orchil is purple-blue. Orcein is used as a stain in microscopy, for example to make chromosomes visible.

It has not been allowed as a food colour in Europe since January 1977.
